canal: You are a resident of this horse-drawn canal town, standing on the near ferry steps because the grain boat that should have come up the cut never arrived. Your cottage is a short walk back along the towpath, and the only food on you is a stale heel of bread in your coat, with a few copper coins and a small knife besides. What you need right now is either a share of flour on this bank or a way across the water before the lock-keeper bars his shed.

The ferry bell above the post is silent. Its rope has been cut short, the end black and frayed, and it gives nothing when the wind moves it. Across the canal you can see the far landing as clearly as a room: a grey horse still in the traces, a ferryman in a patched coat holding a sack, and a woman waving her arm. You hear their voices. You cannot make out one word. Your own lifted hand brings no answer you can trust, and nothing you do from here becomes a sign they recognise.

Bram Holt, the lock-keeper, fills the doorway of the rope shed. He is broad and older, smelling of tar and wet wool, with the spare ferry rope coiled on his arm. "Bell calls the horse," he says, tired rather than cruel. "Without it I don't launch. A false call last month put a horse in the water, and I will not be the man who fails them again." Behind him the shed is still open. A small skiff knocks against the piles, tied and ready, and he has not yet put the bar across.

The towpath is empty of boats. The sacks that should stand by these steps are gone with the failed supply line, and the mill further along this bank will shut when the light goes. Anyone still holding flour is keeping it. The water has turned copper. If Bram bars that door, the skiff and the rope stay his until morning, and morning may come with an empty cupboard. If you spend the last light arguing and get nothing, you also lose the walk to the mill.

You have to choose while that door is open and the mill has not yet locked. Talk him into the rope and you might still cross before dark. Leave the water and you may still get flour, but you give up the skiff. No call you make toward the far bank will be understood, however close the horse and the sack look.

The east bank stayed as sharp as a painted board in the last of the light. The grey horse stamped, and the woman at its head set both hands on the bridle and spoke into its ear. Her voice carried. It broke on the wind and reached you as sound only, no word you could swear to.

The ferryman in the patched coat shifted the sack on his hip. White dust puffed from the open mouth of it and settled on the wet boards of the far landing. That was flour, or what was left of a flour sack, sitting where the missing grain boat should have set it down on this side. He lifted his free hand and shaped his mouth around something urgent. The shape never became a word. A tin cup rang behind him, thin and quick, and even that did not arrange itself into any call you could answer or trust.

You did nothing else. The cut rope on the near bell post lifted once in the wind and fell back, short and black. Nothing you saw crossed the water as a sign either bank would recognise. They were there. You could not make an agreement out of any of it.

Bram Holt watched you not move, and what patience he had thinned with the light. "If you're only looking, I'm barring up," he said. He hung the spare ferry rope on the hook inside the shed and took the iron bar from beside the doorframe. The small skiff knocked once against the piles, still tied, still empty. He had not seated the bar. His hand was on it, and the doorway was narrowing behind his shoulder.

The towpath behind you ran back toward the cottage and on to the mill, where the last flour on this bank would be locked away when the light went. Across the canal the open sack stayed in the ferryman's arms, close enough to see and no use until this bank had a boat in the water or a call the horse would obey. Tar and wet wool hung in the shed mouth. Your pocket still held the stale heel of bread, and your stomach knew it.

You have to choose before that bar drops. Speak, trade, or move now, and you may still get the skiff, the spare rope, or a share at the mill. Wait, and Bram shuts the shed until morning, and morning finds you with that heel of bread and an empty cupboard.
Bram Holt was the nearest person on this bank, broad in the rope-shed doorway with the iron bar in his hand. You asked him what had happened to the bell.

He answered without softening. "Cut. Last night, or the night before. I found it short this morning, and the end burnt so it would not fray clean." He tipped his chin at the black stub on the post. "A false call last month put a horse in the cut. After that I will not launch on a voice. The bell is the call the horse knows. Without it, I do not put the skiff in the water."

Across the canal the ferryman shifted the open sack. White dust lifted off it and settled on the far boards. His mouth worked around something urgent, and the sound came over as noise only. The woman at the grey horse's head lifted her arm. Nothing in the gesture became a sign either bank could trust. You could see them and hear them. You still could not make an answer or an agreement out of any of it.

While he spoke, Bram turned and set the bar across the door. Iron dropped into the slots with a dull knock. The spare ferry rope hung on its hook inside, out of reach, and he turned the key. The small skiff still knocked against the piles. Its painter was tied on the outside of the shed, not behind the bar. He had locked the rope. He had not locked the boat.

"Mill's open a little yet," he said, already half turned toward the towpath. "Flour on this bank, you go now. The boat, you ask me plain, and you do it before I walk home. I am not leaving a launch to a shout I cannot read."

You have to decide now. The shed is shut, and Bram holds the only key to the rope inside it. The skiff is still tied outside and can still be asked for before he leaves. The mill up the towpath may still hand out the last flour on this bank if you get there before it closes. Staying to watch the far bank will not turn their voices into words, and once he is gone the boat sits under his rule until morning.

You stayed on the near steps and did nothing but watch the east bank for a message. The ferryman swung a lantern in a slow arc, three times and then once more, and white dust lifted off the open sack on his hip each time he turned. The woman at the grey horse's head beat a tin cup against a post until the ringing carried over the cut. The light was plain and the sound was plain. None of it became a word, a recognised sign, or an answer either bank could trust.

Bram Holt gave you one last look, broad and tired in the failing dusk. "Then I'm for home," he said, and the key went into his coat with a small hard click. He walked the towpath toward the houses until his back was only a darker shape between the pollarded willows, and the smell of tar and wet wool went with him. The rope shed stayed barred, the spare ferry rope on its hook inside, while the small skiff still knocked at the piles with its painter tied on the outside and nobody left to stop a hand on that rope.

The lane behind the steps did not stay quiet. Two men came into the lamplight arguing over the cut bell, one saying the millers had done it to keep the last flour on this side, the other saying the lock-keepers had shut the water on purpose after the grain boat failed. A woman between them told them to lower their voices before someone got hurt, and neither man stepped back. Their words were this bank's words, close enough to follow. Across the canal the lantern kept moving, and still nothing in it could be made into an agreement.

The mill's high window was still yellow, though the glow had shrunk to a square no bigger than a shutter, and the wheel beyond it had gone quiet. Cold was coming up off the water, and the heel of bread in your coat would not carry you if the cottage cupboard was as bare as you had left it. You have to decide now, while those things are still within reach: go after Bram for the only key to the rope, put a hand to the unguarded skiff, walk for the mill before that window goes dark, or step into the quarrel before blame becomes a shove. Wait any longer and the key, the flour, and a quiet towpath are gone together.

The landing lamp was a small oil light on a hook by the steps, already burning. You lifted it off, set it on the tall mooring pole, and worked the coat over the glass and off again in a slow count of three. You did it again. The light went dark, bright, dark, bright, dark, bright, and then you held it open so the far bank could see the pattern was finished.

Across the cut the ferryman stopped swinging his own lantern. The woman at the grey horse's head let the tin cup fall still. For a long breath they only stared. Then she took his lantern, raised it, and matched you: covered, uncovered, three times, and held. He did it with her on the next pass, slower, careful, the open flour sack still on his hip. White dust showed in the lamp-glow each time the light came back. That was no longer noise. They had copied the count. A sign had crossed the water and come back the same.

You kept the pattern going until there was no mistake in it. On the third copy the ferryman pointed at the sack, then at the skiff, then covered his light three times more. You could read that much without a word. They had grain. They wanted the boat. The horse stamped, and nobody on that bank shouted a call the animal would not know.

The lane did not take the new light quietly. One of the arguing men swore the three-count was a miller's mark, meant to move the last flour off this bank in the dark. The other said it was a lock-keeper's trick, the same hands that cut the bell. The woman between them told them to look at the pole before they named a thief, and neither man lowered his voice. Their boots came down the lane toward the steps. Behind them the mill window had shrunk to a thin yellow slit. Bram was already a dark shape among the pollarded willows, the shed key in his coat, the spare rope still locked.

You have to decide now, while the copied count still holds and before those two men reach the pole. The skiff is tied and empty, and the far bank has just shown they will meet it. The mill may still give flour if you leave at once. Bram can still be called back, but only if you go after him before his door. If you stay on the lamp, the quarrel arrives first.

You worked the coat over the lamp again in the same slow count of three, then pointed once at the water and once at their landing so the ask was a boat, not another copy for its own sake. Across the cut the woman matched the count. The ferryman matched it too, slower, white dust lifting off the open sack each time his light came back.

He did not take the horse. He shook his head at the grey horse, pointed at a low punt under their landing, and held his lantern open. That was a plain answer. They had read the ask. The horse would not move without the bell it knew. A boat with oars would come instead.

He set the sack in the punt and pushed off. The woman stayed at the horse's head so it would not start at the noise from this bank. The punt's bow turned into the cut. Cold water slapped the piles under your boots. You could see the sack. It was coming. It was not here yet.

The lane did not wait for it. The two men reached the steps with the woman still between them, telling them to look before they named a thief. One called the three-count a miller's mark, meant to move the last flour off this bank in the dark. The other said lock-keepers had cut the bell, and now a light was doing their work. Their boots hit the lower step. Neither one stepped back.

Bram was only a darker shape among the willows, the shed key still in his coat, the spare rope still barred inside. Up the towpath the mill window went from a thin yellow slit to nothing. Whatever flour was still being handed out on this bank was gone for the night. The near skiff knocked at the piles, its painter tied outside, with nobody in it.

You have to decide now. The sack is in a boat that has already left the far landing, and you stand to gain it if that crossing finishes at these steps. You stand to lose the lamp, the signal, and a clear place to land if the two men take the pole before the punt arrives. The locked rope will not help you in the next minute. Bram is still walking away.
harbor: You are a local resident, standing in the REVIEW TEST 3 tide archive, the stone room above the quay where the harbor ledger is kept. You came because Mara Voss, the keeper, sent for every person still written in the book before the evening tide, and your bread token is only good if your name stays on the page.

The open ledger smells of wet ink. One line is already fading: Councillor Hale, the leader this settlement relied on, gone three days and now being finished by the water. Mara keeps her hand on the page so she alone will remember him. A council runner waits by the door with the evening bread sack and will not open it until you mark that you accept the erasure.

If you sign, you eat tonight and Hale's name is gone from every mouth but hers. If you refuse, the runner takes your share and the council will call it defiance before the tide finishes the line. You have to choose before the water reaches the step.

You turn to the open door. The nearest neighbour is Ada, from the lower cottages, standing on the quay step in a salt-stiff coat, drawn by the same warm bread smell that is tightening your stomach. You ask which names she still remembers.

She names the living easily — the baker, the boatwright, you — then stalls on Councillor Hale, mouth working as if the face has already gone soft. Mara does not look up from the fading line. "Elsie Penn, the net-mender," she says. "The tide took her last month. I am the only one who can still say it."

The runner cinches the sack shut. Bread smell hangs in the wet room, and he will not open it for talk. The water is on the second step. You still have to choose: mark Hale's erasure and eat, leaving only Mara to remember him, or refuse and lose tonight's share before the tide finishes the line.

You call anyone still in earshot up onto the rise above the archive, clear of the climbing water, and Ada comes at once with two neighbours from the lower cottages. You ask them to say the names they still hold. They agree on the baker and the boatwright, then go quiet on Councillor Hale, one after another, as if the face has already washed thin. Salt wind cuts the warm bread smell off the tied sack.

Mara climbs last with the harbor ledger hugged to her chest, and the council runner plants himself on the path beside her. "The council does not wait on a hill," he says. "You mark Hale's line, or nobody on this rise eats tonight."
The tide is loud on the quay below. You have to decide now: give the mark and keep a share, or hold Hale's name in living mouths and lose the sack.

The path steepened on wet grass. You kept walking until the quay noise thinned, and Ada and the two neighbours came with you, coats snapping in the salt wind. Below, the water slid over the third step and no higher. You were clear of it.

The runner did not follow. He turned the tied sack toward the council path, and the bread smell went with him. "Mark it before I reach the yard," he called, "or the shares go back in the store, and the council writes you as the one who held a crowd on the hill." Mara stayed, the harbor ledger tight to her chest. Hale's line was a pale smear. On the lower path more neighbours had gathered, some blaming the council for taking the bread, some blaming you for keeping them hungry.
You have to choose before the runner reaches the yard: mark Hale and lose him to Mara's memory alone, or let the sack go and face a hungry night with the hill already arguing.

You cupped your hands and called down the rise: Hale walked the quay at dawn, counted the boats, and left the lamp lit for late crews. The argument broke. A woman repeated the lamp, and a man said Hale had promised the evening bread would not skip a tide.

Lanterns swung onto the quay path below—three council searchers calling for the ledger and the crowd that would not mark it. Their boots slapped the wet boards, and the bread smell was already gone toward the yard. Mara gripped the book tighter. "If they take this before the line is copied, I am the only mouth left for him."

The searchers will reach this rise in minutes, and the sack will reach the store first. You must choose now: chase the bread and the mark, stay and face the search while people still say Hale's name, or get the ledger off the hill before they close the path.

You crouched and asked who was still sure. Ada named the baker, and the boatwright's neighbour agreed; nobody would write Hale. With no page of your own, a woman tore a strip from a wrapping and held it on her knee while you copied those two names in charcoal from a cold stick.

The salt wind smeared the letters. Lanterns reached the first bend below, and a searcher called for the ledger and the crowd. Mara looked at the strip. "That keeps the living. It does not keep him." The runner was already gone toward the yard with the bread.

You must choose before they crest the rise: show the strip, hide it, or leave the hill and chase the sack. If you show only two names, they may still take Mara's book. If you chase the sack, the searchers reach her first.
guided: You are a hardened survivor, sheltering in a cracked stone watch-hut above the trade road, where you brought your sister Mara to keep her out of the drought camps. She stands in the doorway, one sleeve dark with blood, and says the road-warden is already at the bend below.

He wants the hidden spring you swore never to name, or he takes her down the hill tonight. Speak it and you spend the only secret that still buys you safety. Stay quiet, and he climbs before her arm stops bleeding.
Mara shook her head. She had only said she was bleeding and looking for kin. She never named the spring.

More than one voice carried up from the bend. People on the trade road were shouting at the road-wardens about the dried wells, and the man below answered them as if a crowd already stood with him. He still wants the spring tonight, or he takes Mara down into that noise before dark.
You lean into the doorway and call that you will talk, but he must stay on the path. The road-warden stops halfway up, spear planted in the dust, near enough to hear and not near enough to seize her.
He shouts the debt where the yelling crowd can hear: show him the hidden spring tonight, or he takes Mara down the hill before dark. Answer now, or he starts to climb.
The cloth bit into Mara's sleeve and slowed the warm seep under your thumb. You stepped back, and the doorway went empty.

The road-warden saw that and started up, spear low, not running yet. Dust rose behind him. Hold the hut, meet him before the door, or take the back trail. Stay, and he is at the threshold in moments. Run, and the spring stays unnamed, but her arm will open again on the slope.
